https://english.radio.cz/summer-film-sch.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Summer Film School honours Ester Krumbachová Facebook Twitter This year's Summer Film School in Uherské Hradiště is paying tribute to Ester Krumbachová, one of the most influential figures of the Czechoslovak New Wave. Best known as a costume designer, screenwriter and the director of The Murder of Mr. Devil, she helped shape classics such as Daisies and Diamonds of the Night. Alongside screenings of films she worked on, the festival has opened an exhibition featuring photographs by Libuše Jarcovjáková, costume designs, jewellery, amulets and personal documents. Organisers say the retrospective offers a comprehensive look at Krumbachová's lasting influence on Czech and Czechoslovak cinema. Photograph: imageBROKER.com/Alamy View image in fullscreen Familiar face … the Skanderbeg Tower is designed to echo a bust of Albania’s national hero. Photograph: imageBROKER.com/Alamy Architecture ‘Starchitects go home’: what’s the truth behind Albania’s astonishing building boom? Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’ Oliver Wainwright Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.15 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google L ast autumn, I was sitting with a prominent architect in New York, when their phone wouldn’t stop buzzing. They finally checked the messages and chuckled. “Oh, the Albanian Architecture Army chat is blowing up again,” they said. “It looks like Edi has some new projects for us.” Edi was Edi Rama, the prime minister of Albania since 2013, who has been presiding over the rapid transformation of the former communist country with a fleet of glamorous building projects. There are twisting towers in Tirana, along with prize-winning public spaces , striking coastal resorts, and many more dazzling visions on the way – all now brought together in a hefty new book, The Albanian Files . Critics see the 800-page book as a 2.2kg dossier of evidence The country’s makeover, it turns out, is partly coordinated via a WhatsApp group (“Albanian ArchArmy” for short) which includes some of the most famous architects in the world. It is a forum where achievements are shared, new projects celebrated, and the great prime minister-patron showered with praise for his bravery and boldness. The New York architect describes the situation in the manner of a superhero movie: Rama sends out the signal and the world’s starchitects rally to the rescue with their daring designs. Look hard enough and you might even see the Albanian double-headed eagle projected into the night sky. View image in fullscreen Hub … Saranda port development plan by XDGA, shown in The Albanian Files. Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller Publishers The WhatsApp chat might be confidential, but The Albanian Files is the next best thing. It is a remarkable document, in ways that are both intended and not. In his foreword, Rama describes the book as “a precious behind-the-scenes record” of a process that is “lifting Albania in a way that nobody saw coming”. It is an eye-opening directory of dreams, in which 60 international practices (and not a single Albanian one) lay out their plans for over 500 projects up and down the country. To Rama’s critics, however, the book is an 800-page, 2.2kg dossier of evidence. They point to the opacity of decision-making , the destruction of heritage , the forced evictions , the trampling of protected landscapes , and the role of Albania’s construction industry in laundering money for organised crime . The publication is full of first-hand testimonies by architects documenting their experiences, and one opposition MP has called it the “smoking gun” – although there is no suggestion that the architects have been involved in any wrongdoing. Rama is right that nobody saw it coming: most of the projects in the book’s pages are news to the local population, which has reacted with fury. “Starchitects go home!” read one placard at a noisy protest in June , outside a venue in Tirana, where many of the architects in the book were gathered for an exclusive event to celebrate their work and launch the publication. “Where is the public?” read another. Tickets for the architecture festival, titled Landscapes of Abundance , cost up to €200, in a country where the median monthly wage is €700. It came at a charged moment, just a few weeks after huge national protests were ignited by the multibillion dollar plans to develop Zvërnec nature reserve and the nearby island of Sazan into a luxury resort , backed by the Trump family. Dubbed the flamingo revolution , in reference to the fragile habitats critics say will be trampled by the project, the protests have now continued for over 120 days, with ever-louder calls for Rama’s resignation. Architecture has found itself unexpectedly in the firing line. View image in fullscreen Anger … Albanians protest at development of coastal nature reserve in June this year. Photograph: Armando Babani/Getty Images “It feels like living in an autocratic kingdom,” says Lorin Kadiu, director of Citizens.al , an investigative news platform that has been tracking construction projects in Albania since 2018. “Not just the lack of transparency, but the fact that we must all be subjected to the aesthetic tastes of one person. The whole country must be painted the way he wants.” Rama, who trained as a painter, first rose to prominence as the mayor of Tirana in the 2000s, when he made international headlines with his programme of painting the dreary soviet blocks a rainbow of jaunty colours . The cheap and cheerful makeover worked, and Rama was hailed for his maverick artistic approach. But, now, many of his former supporters feel like his architectural ambitions have gone too far. An open letter , handed out at the protests, denounced the “art-washing of bulldozer politics,” and asked the assembled architects if they enjoy “the freedom to do here what would be forbidden, challenged, or otherwise made impossible in your own countries?” Of the architects contacted by the Guardian, only one responded, to say they do not do anything in Albania that they would not be allowed to do in another place. They added that “the freedom in Albania is certainly alluring and as such the personal responsibility is greater”. As Rama writes pointedly in his foreword to The Albanian Files, the architects are attracted to work in Albania by the “freedom from ‘no’ in all its forms”. The pages are studded with visions for virgin coastlines, verdant forests, and pristine dunes and lagoons. In Gjipe, a bay that many consider the last virgin beach in southern Albania, Dutch firm MVRDV has proposed a mirrored glass hotel that would span the gorge , “like a jewel on the coastline”. It comes hot on the heels of their apartment tower in Tirana shaped like the head of Skanderbeg , Albania’s national hero (which also bears a striking resemblance to Rama). In the protected dune area of Rana e Hedhun, the venerable Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza has masterplanned a hillside development with a cable car and a tower-block on the beach . A few pages later, Swiss maestro Valerio Olgiati proposes a cluster of concrete towers rising from the sand, peppered with defensive windows . It looks as if he might be preparing to fend off an invasion from the sea. The coastal glow-up continues with the Florentine luxury yacht designer Luca Dini (studio mission: “to astonish even the most discerning”). He presents an illustrated voyage through his 17 projects, including the Life Marina Complex, spanning seven kilometres of virgin coastline near Saranda, and the Atara resort, with a golden “crown” that hovers above the cliffs like another military lookout post. It almost reaches parody when his comic-style illustrations conclude with an image of a super-yacht hurtling above a skyline, with the designer himself declaiming from the deck: “[we] create spaces that harmonise with the environment.” View image in fullscreen Comic-style illustrations … Luca Dini’s section in The Albanian Files. Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller Publishers The book’s editor, Anneke Abhelakh, asked the architects to submit their own texts, and they are striking in their honesty. At times it reads like a hot-mic transcript. “Because there are not many rules and my clients care very little for the context,” writes Berlin-based architect Sam Chermayeff, “we are forced to think through our own values.” He recounts the “truly wild” experience of working in Albania, including how he was called, out of the blue, by one of Rama’s associates, and soon asked to design two towers in Tirana , totalling 45,000sq m – quite something for a designer better known for experimental kitchens. “Of course I agreed,” he adds, “not really understanding what was happening.” Contacted for comment, Chermayeff responded: “I do ask Albanian clients the same questions that I ask of clients in any country and am equally assured,” adding that “as in Germany or the US, I really do not know more than what I am told,” and that he does not work in or near protected areas. “I do not do anything,” he added, “I would not do at another place.” Austrian architect Chris Precht describes how he was approached on Instagram by Rama himself, “asking if I would be interested in working in Albania”. He now has 29 projects to his name, including a €4m “ Garden of Eden ”, built in the courtyard of the prime minister’s own office. “It is an unimaginable reality,” says a campaign group of Albanian architects and urban planners, Arkitektët Shqiparë , which has created an online database of all of the projects – published in Albanian, unlike the book. “A narrow group of foreign architects is contacted directly by the prime minister’s office and receives projects without a competitive procedure.” View image in fullscreen Beside the seaside … Olgiati’s proposal for concrete towers on the beach in Lezha. Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller Publishers The foreign architects describe it differently. “Rama never appoints the architects himself,” one member of the ArchArmy group tells me. “But he makes introductions to developers. And it is understood that, if they choose one of his architects, they [the developers] will get permission to build what they want.” Rama has consistently denied the allegations. In a furious interview with CNN in June, he denounced the claims of corruption as “ fake news ”. He has long maintained that the wider protests have been stoked by the US president’s enemies , including Iran. “If it were not Jared Kushner,” he said, “nobody would give a shit about flamingos, about Albania, about nothing. It’s the whole hate against Trump that creates all this scrutiny.” Contacted by the Guardian, the prime minister’s office did not respond to requests for comment in detail but called the allegations “hearsays” and “bitter assessments”. During a speech this week to launch the competition for a new tower, Rama insisted the competition juries are “mostly architects, urbanists and academics who are entirely free,” that “the Albanian side is in the minority” and that there is “never any orientation or influence” on the jury. He added that today Albania “is the largest open ‘university’ in architecture,” as young Albanian architects have the opportunity “to meet, to follow, to work concretely with masters”. The book’s subtitle is Freedom and Architecture, and there is an air of carte blanche to many of the designs. “Working as an architect in Albania is liberating,” writes the Belgian Xaveer De Geyter, alongside his proposal for a colossal trio of M-shaped towers for the port of Saranda, “provoking a degree of freedom that sometimes leaves us in a cold sweat.” Spanish studio Arquitectura-G praises Albania’s permitting process as “significantly faster and less restrictive” than elsewhere, driven by “a clear vision coming from the prime minister.” Portugal’s Manuel Aires Mateus concurs: “There are times when things have to be top-down.” The palpable thrill of building on virgin terrain is also evident. Japanese doyen Kengo Kuma describes the exhilaration of flying over Albania in a helicopter. “I found it very exciting,” he writes, “as most of the nature is untouched.” In Asia, he adds, “it is very difficult to find a project in such ‘virgin land’”. The Berlin-based Indian architect, Anupama Kundoo, talks of the opportunity to create, “free from the baggage” of Europe and other “developed countries”. Kundoo is working on a masterplan for a “laboratory settlement” of 50,000 people in the protected Divjakë-Karavasta national park . Such a project has only been made possible by a controversial 2024 law, which allows the construction of five-star resorts in protected areas, from which the Trump-backed plan in Zvërnec also benefits. There is no suggestion that any of the architects named in this article are breaking any laws. “The developers are in a hurry,” says Kadiu. “There is a sprint to build as much as possible before these laws are repealed.” Pressure is growing. Albania has entered the concluding phase of its EU accession negotiations, but these lax regulations remain an obstacle. Both the 2024 law, and 2015 legislation that gives preferential treatment to “strategic investors”, were criticised by an EU report last year as being in conflict with its standards. A European Parliament resolution in June this year “ expressed serious concerns ” and called for an “immediate moratorium on new permitting procedures, construction works and development interventions” within protected areas. Rama continues to defend both laws as pragmatic, modernising policies that balance environmental conservation with high-value economic development. Beyond fears for the environment, and the opaque permitting and procurement processes, another burning question remains: how can one of the poorest countries in Europe afford to build these extravagant schemes? There has been an astronomical rise in property prices, but no comparable increase in wages or bank mortgages being issued, leading critics to suspect that dark money is involved. The Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime identifies Albania’s real estate and tourism sectors as major sites of money-laundering, noting that the construction sector is “ heavily infiltrated by illicit funds ”. Its 2020 report estimated that €1.6bn of “dirty money” had been laundered through Albanian real estate in the previous three years. As I reported in 2022 , leaked wiretaps revealed Italian mafia figures discussing how Tirana’s high-rise boom was a prime opportunity for laundering their cash, with construction prices of roughly €500 per sq m paling in comparison to the listing prices of up to €4,000 per sq m. Albania’s own Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organized Crime, SPAK, is making progress. In June, it seized €150m of assets , including apartments, villas and commercial properties, tied to an alleged cocaine trafficking network. The same month, Pëllumb Gjoka, once named a “strategic investor” by the Albanian government with approval to build a €52m resort on the coast, was sent to prison for ordering mob hits . View image in fullscreen ‘It’s a classic example of what happens when you think you’re the benevolent leader’ … Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. Photograph: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images Research by Citizens.al shows that several projects in The Albanian Files are linked to ongoing SPAK investigations (none of the architects named in this article are implicated), alleging criminal capital has been funnelled through shell companies, construction contracts and property transactions . Over 40% of the projects in the book don’t even mention who the client is, leading many to ask: why the opacity? One former member of the ArchArmy is rueful about the way things have turned out. “Like the others, I joined with a real conviction that this could be a positive change for the country,” they tell me. “Rama knew Albania was going to develop very quickly, and he didn’t want to fuck it up. It’s better to have some good architects involved to make sure it turns out halfway decent, rather than people building generic apartments along the coast without any control.” The architect says they backed out after being part of a competition jury that “didn’t feel democratic” and the fact that issues around land ownership “always felt very vague”. Photo: Courtesy of Pinglu Canal Group The newly opened Pinglu Canal in South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region has become a focal point of discussion for industry experts from home and abroad at the ongoing World Canals Conference 2026 (WCC) in Guilin, Guangxi, as many hailed the canal's economic value, engineering feats and ecological contribution. The conference runs from Monday to Friday in Guilin. Notably, this year's event closely follows the recent opening of the Pinglu Canal, which is also located in the autonomous region in South China. The 134.2-kilometer Pinglu Canal is the first canal planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949 to connect a river to the sea, and it opens up the shortest, most economical, and most convenient sea outlet for southwestern China. It is a backbone project of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor that connects with the China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative and marks a major addition to the nation's river network. The project has set four world records among comparable canals: the highest navigation capacity, the fastest ship-lock transit speed, the highest lift for a water-saving ship lock, and the largest water-saving ship lock on an inland waterway. As hundreds of canal experts from home and abroad gathered in Guilin, the Pinglu Canal's engineering achievements as well as other features such as ecological protection, were constantly acknowledged by participants in the event. "There is something quite remarkable about witnessing the beginning of an entirely new canal corridor," Sharon Leighton, president of Inland Waterways International, said at the opening ceremony of the event on Tuesday. "The Pinglu Canal introduces a new chapter in the long story of populations using waterways to connect and create opportunity." "Of everything I know, this is remarkable and leading," Leighton told the Global Times on Monday, commenting on the canal's engineering achievements in solving technical difficulties. Tomas Kolark, a canal expert from the Czech Republic, told the Global Times that the Pinglu Canal is very impressive in terms of engineering and water management. "I was watching closely the preparations and mainly the construction of the canal, and it was very interesting to see it now with my own eyes," Kolark said. "Another interesting approach of the canal was, for example, it is maybe one of the world's first bridges for wildlife crossings." As a project built with protecting the environment and ecology in mind, the Pinglu Canal has built fish passages, animal bridges and bird corridors, reflecting a deliberate effort to harmonize infrastructure with nature, the Global Times learned from Pinglu Canal Group, the builder of the canal. "It was interesting to see that 98 percent of the material excavated from the canal's construction was used for construction purposes. In all, it's very interesting to see how the canal was planned and built, and we could see today how it's used," said Kolark. Eddie Lee, a participant in the event, told the Global Times that she learned through visits to some of the hubs along the Pinglu Canal, where she saw how engineers tackled the difficulties in managing the high-water lift. She also understood the special technology used on the ship lock's gates to ensure smooth opening and closing while withstanding the high pressure. "It's interesting to know that Chinese engineers have worked with academia and top technology universities to tackle the issues," Lee said. "I understand that it will be very important for the economy in Guangxi, in [Southwest China's] Guizhou Province, and in [Southwest China's] Yunnan Province. I have traveled a lot in China, seeing that some southern parts have not developed as fast as northern or eastern parts. I think the Pinglu Canal will make a big difference." For its achievement, the Pinglu Canal Project was awarded the Green Design International Award by the World Green Design Organization on Tuesday, according to the Beijing-based stdaily.com. https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-ho.text: Spain will grind to a halt in its first general strike in 14 years on Wednesday, just weeks before voters head to the polls in a snap election . At the center of both the strike and vote, one issue looms especially large: unaffordable housing . Anger over the crisis boiled over in September, following the eviction of an elderly woman from the Madrid home in which she had lived since 1956. Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in nationwide protests, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to submit a long-delayed housing bill to the Spanish parliament. When lawmakers rejected the legislation, he decided to send voters to the polls. “Every generation has its struggle,” Sánchez said during a rally shortly after calling the snap vote. “Ours is housing, and we will solve it, backed by the strength of the people.” Advertisement Advertisement “We must look upwards at those in the penthouses and those who run vulture funds and put an end to their speculative practices and abuses,” he added, calling for voters to unite to protect “small property owners and tenants.” It is no wonder Sánchez has attempted to seize on the topic of housing in a bid to be reelected. The high price of homes is at the forefront of voters’ minds: the most recent data shows house prices are double what they were at the same time in 2015; the average Spaniard doesn’t leave their parental home until after their 30 th birthday ; and in some historic centers tourist accommodation accounts for 45% of the rental market . His big challenge, however, is that he could end up blamed for the problem exploding during his more than eight years in office. Between 2015 and 2025, average home prices in Spain rose by 80% , while salaries increased by only 30%. A pledge to use “all state resources” to provide 184,000 public and affordable rental homes has been difficult to realize. And yet, on many metrics, Spain’s housing struggles are not even the worst in Europe. Rising rents and home prices across the bloc are fueling discontent and setting the stage for affordability to become a key issue in a string of elections set for the coming year. Here’s everything you need to know: Between 2015 and 2025, house prices in Spain rose 80%, according to Eurostat’s house price index. The first half of 2026 made this figure even starker: by the second quarter of this year, prices were around double what they were at the same time in 2015. Advertisement Advertisement Rents have also risen across the country, with urban regions and tourist hotspots seeing some of the biggest rent hikes over the past 10 years. Academics trace the roots of Spain’s housing crisis to the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis: while ordinary homebuyers struggled to get mortgages, large-scale investors began buying up property, speculating and driving up prices. “The cash didn’t disappear from the market; it just ended up in the hands of investors,” said Spanish National Research Council housing expert Javier Gil. “What we see in Spain is a new cycle led by speculative, non-residential demand.” Combine that with growing populations in major cities, social housing stock issues, and tourist housing, which the national bank estimates accounts for about 10% of the already small rental market, and Spaniards really feel the pinch. Young people make up one of the key groups struggling to find their place in the Spanish housing market. In 2025, 67% of people aged between 18 and 34 still lived with their parents and almost half of the 26-34-year-olds in this position cited the inability to afford to rent or buy as the principal reason for their living situation. “The prices just keep rising and rising, and landlords take advantage of the system to take advantage of tenants,” said Jorge Collado, a 26-year-old who took part in a massive protest encampment housing demonstrators set up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square. Advertisement Advertisement The university student said he had been forced to move back to his family’s home after his former landlord dramatically raised the monthly rent when he requested a legal rental contract. “We’re fed up with this situation, and the politicians aren’t doing anything to solve this.” Although stark, Spain’s house price increases are not even the highest in Europe, Research Director at Housing Europe Alice Pittini warns, pointing to Eastern European countries that have seen “tremendous increases” in recent years. Similarly, rents increased in every EU member state between 2025 and the first half of this year. In fact, rent rises across Spain during this period were relatively modest compared with most other EU countries, when national averages are considered. While Sánchez has bet his career on converting public anger over housing into votes for his party, it will be a difficult sell given the price rises during his time in office. “Changes in housing policy have the tendency to see the impact of the policies […] much, much later. So it’s something that I think is always a tricky field for politicians,” Pittini points out. Given that the housing problem is plaguing various other European countries and has already taken center stage in local elections in Berlin and national elections in the Netherlands, it seems set to remain at the top of the agenda as many Europeans prepare to go to the polls next year.
